stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about manual pedestrian counts?
stimulus: City planners have traditionally estimated pedestrian volume with manual counts: staff stationed at an intersection tally passersby for a few hours on a chosen weekday. In Valmont, planner Odile Marchetti compared such counts with a year of readings from sidewalk sensors installed along the Calder Street corridor. The two methods agreed closely on weekday mornings. However, the sensors recorded late-evening and weekend foot traffic on several blocks that was nearly double the weekday peaks the manual counts had captured, during hours that no scheduled count had ever covered.
choices: They fail to measure pedestrian volume accurately at any time of day, even during the hours they cover.
They can miss periods of heavy use on some blocks, since they cover only a few scheduled hours.
They can miss periods of heavy use on some blocks, since staff tend to miscount during busy hours.
They tend to overstate weekend foot traffic on blocks where weekday traffic is relatively light.
explanation: The pivot at 'However' tells you what the comparison found: the counts matched the sensors when they were taken, but the heaviest traffic came at evenings and weekends, 'hours that no scheduled count had ever covered.' Go one step past that and you get the implication: because manual counts sample only limited windows, they can leave out the busiest periods.

A.why: You turned a limitation into a total failure. The text says the two methods 'agreed closely on weekday mornings,' so the counts were accurate for the hours they covered. Their weakness is what they leave out.

C.why: You read the first half, which is correct, and stopped. The reason it gives is wrong: the counts matched the sensors during the hours they were taken, so miscounting isn't the issue. The issue is the hours they never covered.

D.why: This reverses the finding. No manual count covered weekends at all, and the sensors showed weekend traffic was higher than the counts suggested, so nothing was overstated.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the predator-loss explanation for urchin barrens?
stimulus: Purple sea urchins sometimes graze kelp forests down to bare rock, and the usual explanation credits the disappearance of predators such as sea otters. Biologist Tomas Reyna's team compared reefs off two islands where otters had been absent for decades. On one, urchins had stripped the kelp entirely; on the other, kelp persisted, and the team found that strong winter swells there regularly knocked urchins loose from the rock. Where swells were weak, barrens spread regardless of whether predatory fish were abundant.
choices: It is mistaken, because predators have no measurable effect on the size of urchin populations.
It is incomplete, because predatory fish appear to keep urchins in check where otters are absent.
It best accounts for kelp persisting on reefs where strong winter swells regularly occur.
It is incomplete, because physical conditions also appear to influence whether barrens form.
explanation: Otters were missing from both islands, yet only one island had a barren, and the difference was the swells. So predator loss can't be the whole story. The one-step inference is that the explanation is incomplete because physical conditions matter too. Nothing in the text says predators don't matter at all.

A.why: You went two steps instead of one. The study shows another factor is involved, not that predators have no effect. Neither reef had otters, so the study couldn't test what otters do.

B.why: The first half is right and the second half is wrong. The last sentence says barrens spread 'regardless of whether predatory fish were abundant,' so the fish didn't keep urchins in check.

C.why: This credits the predator explanation with a result that actually came from the swells. Otters were absent from that reef too. The kelp survived because waves knocked the urchins loose.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the early twentieth-century collectors who visited Kerlouan?
stimulus: Residents of the Breton village of Kerlouan have long described the dance tune "An Hini Kozh" as older than the parish church, and collectors who visited in the early 1900s dutifully recorded it as such. Musicologist Anaïs Le Goff notes, however, that the melody depends on a raised fourth scale degree common in printed quadrilles of the 1840s and absent from every earlier manuscript from the region. The villagers' account, she argues, may say more about the tune's place in local identity than about its actual age.
choices: They wrote down the villagers' claim about the tune's age without testing it against other evidence.
They deliberately exaggerated the tune's age in order to make their collections seem more valuable.
They accepted the villagers' account after comparing the tune with earlier regional manuscripts.
They were chiefly interested in how the tune expressed the village's sense of local identity.
explanation: Look at how the collectors are framed: they 'dutifully recorded' what residents said, and Le Goff then finds evidence the collectors apparently never checked. The ironic 'dutifully' implies they passed on local tradition without testing it. That is as far as the text goes.

B.why: You read uncritical recording as deliberate deception. The text suggests the collectors were too trusting, but it says nothing about motive or intent to mislead.

C.why: Le Goff's evidence comes from the earlier manuscripts, and the tune's feature is missing from all of them. If the collectors had made that comparison, they couldn't have accepted the villagers' claim.

D.why: This gives Le Goff's conclusion to the wrong people. The point about local identity is her modern reading of the claim. The collectors simply recorded the tune as old.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about food-frequency questionnaires?
stimulus: Large studies of diet usually rely on food-frequency questionnaires, in which participants estimate how often they ate various foods over the past year. In a trial led by nutrition scientist Priya Haldar, 400 adults completed such questionnaires and also provided urine samples analyzed for nitrogen, a reliable marker of protein intake. For most participants, questionnaire estimates tracked the biomarker reasonably well. Adults with higher body weights, however, reported on average about 20 percent less protein than their samples indicated.
choices: They cannot provide useful information about how much protein study participants eat.
They may skew results for some groups, because people forget foods eaten long ago.
They may underestimate protein intake for certain groups of participants in a consistent way.
They tend to overestimate protein intake among participants with higher body weights.
explanation: The questionnaires mostly worked, but one identifiable group under-reported protein by a similar margin on average. One step beyond that: the error isn't random. It runs in one direction for certain groups, so questionnaires may underestimate their intake consistently.

A.why: You took a limitation and made it absolute. For most participants the estimates 'tracked the biomarker reasonably well,' so the questionnaires do provide useful information.

B.why: The first half fits the text, but the cause doesn't come from it. The text never explains why the gap appears, and forgetting would affect everyone, not one weight group in particular.

D.why: This flips the direction. Those participants reported less protein than their samples showed, which is an underestimate.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about forest reconstructions based on fossil pollen?
stimulus: Reconstructions of ancient forests have relied heavily on fossil pollen, which accumulates in lake sediments in enormous quantities. Yet some trees, including larches, shed pollen grains that are fragile and seldom preserved. When paleobotanist Henrik Solvang examined needles and cones recovered from Norwegian lake cores, he found larch remains in layers dating to 9,000 years ago, a period for which the pollen record from the same cores shows almost no larch at all.
choices: They are too unreliable to show which tree species grew in ancient forests.
They may underrepresent tree species whose pollen rarely survives in sediment.
They may underrepresent larches, because pollen is scarcer in lake sediments than needles are.
They have overstated how common larches were in Norwegian forests 9,000 years ago.
explanation: The 'Yet' sentence names the weakness: some trees' pollen 'seldom' survives. The needles and cones then show larches were there when the pollen record says they weren't. The careful inference is that pollen records may undercount species with fragile pollen.

A.why: You read a gap for some species as a failure of the whole method. The text names one problem group, trees with fragile pollen. It doesn't say pollen fails to identify trees in general.

C.why: The opening is right, but the reason contradicts the first sentence, which says pollen accumulates 'in enormous quantities.' Larch pollen is missing because it is fragile, not because pollen in general is scarce.

D.why: This is the wrong direction. The pollen record showed almost no larch while the needles and cones showed larches were present, so the pollen understated them.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about visual surface inspections of concrete bridge decks?
stimulus: Engineers often judge the health of a concrete bridge deck by inspecting its surface for cracks. In 2019, inspectors rated the deck of the Harlan River viaduct in good condition after finding only hairline surface cracking. Two years later, a ground-penetrating radar survey revealed that chloride from road salt had corroded the reinforcing steel across a third of the deck, beneath concrete that still looked sound. Repairs estimated at $2 million in 2019 ultimately cost $9 million.
choices: They can miss hidden deterioration that would have been less costly to repair if found sooner.
They are of no real value to engineers trying to assess the condition of a bridge deck.
They can miss hidden deterioration, since hairline cracks are usually too fine for inspectors to see.
They are designed mainly to detect the kinds of damage that road salt causes in concrete.
explanation: Each sentence adds a piece: inspectors saw a sound-looking surface, the corrosion was underneath, and the cost rose from $2 million to $9 million. Together they imply that surface inspections can miss internal damage, and that catching it late made it more expensive to fix.

B.why: You moved from 'can miss something' to 'useless.' One case of missed corrosion shows the method has a blind spot. It doesn't show the method has no value.

C.why: The first half matches the answer, but the second half fails. The inspectors did find the hairline cracks. What they missed was corrosion beneath 'concrete that still looked sound.'

D.why: The text never says what surface inspections are designed for. If anything, salt damage was exactly what this inspection failed to catch.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the claims made by nineteenth-century print dealers?
stimulus: Nineteenth-century dealers in Japanese woodblock prints routinely advertised "first editions," assuring buyers that the brilliant blues of their impressions proved the prints came from the earliest runs, before the blocks had worn. Conservator Mei Tanabe's analysis of 120 impressions of a single Hiroshige design complicates that sales pitch. Blue intensity varied widely even among impressions with identical, crisply cut lines, and several of the most vivid examples came from late printings in which the block had visibly cracked.
choices: The dealers knowingly sold late impressions as early ones in order to charge higher prices.
Color was a less dependable sign, because blue pigments fade unevenly as prints age.
The most vivid impressions usually came from the earliest runs, just as the dealers maintained.
Color was a less dependable sign of an early impression than the dealers led buyers to believe.
explanation: The text reports the dealers' assurances without endorsing them. Calling them a 'sales pitch' signals the distance. Tanabe's data then show vivid blues in late, cracked printings. The one-step inference is that color was a weaker sign of an early impression than the dealers claimed.

A.why: You went from 'the claim was unreliable' to 'the dealers lied on purpose.' The text questions their evidence. It says nothing about what they knew or intended.

B.why: The first half is right, but fading is your own explanation. Tanabe found variation at the time of printing, including vivid late impressions, and the text never mentions pigments changing over time.

C.why: You took the dealers' claim as the author's view and missed the ironic framing. Tanabe found 'several of the most vivid examples' among late printings.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about clinic-based reporting of flu cases?
stimulus: Public health agencies typically gauge a city's flu activity by counting positive tests reported by clinics. Because many people with mild symptoms never see a doctor, epidemiologist Ruth Okafor's team began sampling wastewater in Dunmore, where material from every connected household reaches a single treatment plant. During the 2024 season, viral levels in the wastewater rose about ten days before clinic reports did. The team cautions that wastewater cannot show who is infected, but it may give officials an earlier signal that an outbreak is beginning.
choices: It fails to detect flu outbreaks and could therefore be replaced by wastewater sampling.
It registers a rise late, because clinics are slow to send their test results to agencies.
It tends to register a rise in flu activity some time after that rise begins in the community.
It identifies which individuals are infected less precisely than wastewater sampling does.
explanation: The wastewater rose 'about ten days before clinic reports did,' and the team calls it a possible 'earlier signal.' One step beyond that: clinic reports pick up an outbreak only after it has already started spreading. Notice the hedges, 'may' and 'cautions.' The text doesn't claim more than a lag.

A.why: This is the absolute trap. Clinic reports did detect the rise, just later. The team's caution that wastewater 'cannot show who is infected' also rules out replacing clinics.

B.why: The first half is supported, but the reason isn't. The text points to people with mild symptoms never seeing a doctor. It never says clinics are slow to send results.

D.why: This reverses the comparison. The text says wastewater 'cannot show who is infected,' so clinic testing is the more precise of the two for identifying individuals.
